lessonTitle: Core Practical Procedures: Safe Performance with Consent

blocks.text: A third-year student is asked to cannulate a frightened 74-year-old before her antibiotics. He is confident about the vein but has not checked which arm was used for a mastectomy, has not introduced himself, and has left the sharps bin on the other side of the bed. Technique is the easy part; safe procedure is a habit made of consent, preparation and aftercare.

blocks.markdown: **Principles common to every procedure.** (1) *Indication*: be able to state why the procedure is needed and whether a less invasive option exists. (2) *Consent*: introduce yourself, explain what, why, the main risks and alternatives, and obtain and record valid consent; adults with capacity can refuse. Students perform procedures only under supervision and within their competence. (3) *Preparation*: identify the patient, check allergies (including latex and chlorhexidine), gather equipment, wash hands, position the patient and use good lighting. (4) *Asepsis*: use an aseptic non-touch technique. (5) *Safety*: dispose of sharps at the point of use, never re-sheath needles, and document everything.

blocks.title: Aseptic non-touch technique (ANTT)
blocks.text: A standardised approach to prevent pathogens reaching susceptible sites: hand hygiene, a clean working surface, protecting key parts (needle tip, catheter, connector) so that they never touch non-sterile surfaces, and using sterile gloves where key parts must be touched directly.

blocks.markdown: **Venepuncture and cannulation.** Venepuncture takes blood; cannulation places a short plastic tube in a vein for access. Choose the antecubital fossa (median cubital vein) for venepuncture and a forearm or back-of-hand vein for a cannula. Avoid an arm with an arteriovenous fistula or graft, an arm with a running infusion, and (usually) the side of an axillary lymph node clearance or lymphoedema. Apply the tourniquet no longer than about a minute, clean the skin and allow it to dry, anchor the skin, insert the needle at a shallow angle with the bevel up, release the tourniquet before withdrawing the needle, and apply pressure. Use the order of draw specified by your local laboratory.

rows: Large central or antecubital veins; painful
Major surgery, rapid infusion, blood products
Common first choice for most adults
blocks.caption: Gauge colours follow the international colour code. Flow rates differ by manufacturer, so check the packaging. Choose the smallest gauge that meets the clinical need.

blocks.title: Worked example 1: cannulating a patient who needs intravenous antibiotics
blocks.prompt: Mrs L, 74, has pneumonia and needs a cannula for intravenous antibiotics. She had a right mastectomy with axillary node clearance years ago and is anxious about needles. Describe how you would proceed and record it.

steps.text: Confirm the indication (intravenous therapy cannot be given orally) and check the prescription against local policy; the antibiotic and dose are for the prescriber and must be checked against BNF and local guidance.

Introduce yourself, explain the procedure, risks (pain, bruising, infection, phlebitis, infiltration, occasionally nerve irritation) and alternatives; obtain and record verbal consent. Ask about allergies and which arm she prefers.

Choose the left arm because of the previous right axillary clearance; inspect and palpate for a straight, soft, bouncy vein, apply the tourniquet, clean the skin with an appropriate antiseptic and allow it to dry, anchor the vein, insert at a shallow angle, advance the catheter off the needle when flashback is seen, release the tourniquet, apply pressure over the vein and remove the needle directly into the sharps bin.

Flush with saline to confirm patency (no pain or swelling), secure with a dressing and label with the date, time and operator. Document the site, gauge, number of attempts and any difficulty, and set a daily review of the site and the continued need.

blocks.answer: The cannula is placed in the arm opposite the previous axillary clearance, using ANTT, valid consent and a recorded daily review; sharps are discarded at the point of use.

blocks.markdown: **Urinary catheterisation.** Indications include acute or chronic retention, accurate monitoring of urine output in the critically ill, and some peri-operative and palliative situations; intermittent catheterisation or alternatives are preferred where possible, and every catheter needs a documented reason and a review date to reduce catheter-associated infection. Principles: consent, privacy and chaperone as appropriate, ANTT, lubricating (and anaesthetic) gel in the urethra, and insertion to the hilt in men before the balloon is inflated, only after urine drains, using the recommended volume for the balloon. In men replace the foreskin afterwards to avoid paraphimosis. Do not attempt urethral catheterisation if there is blood at the meatus after pelvic trauma or suspected urethral injury; seek urological advice.

rows: Haematoma, vasovagal syncope, nerve or arterial puncture, infection
Correct site, tourniquet time, pressure afterwards, patient lying down if faint
Phlebitis, infiltration, infection, haematoma, accidental arterial placement
ANTT, secure dressing, daily review, remove when no longer needed
Catheter-associated urinary infection, urethral trauma, false passage, paraphimosis, blockage
ANTT, insertion to the hilt, check urine drains before inflating balloon, review daily, restore foreskin
Haematoma, arterial spasm or occlusion, pain, infection
Check collateral supply, firm pressure for at least five minutes, check perfusion afterwards
blocks.caption: Complications and mitigation for the core procedures.
Henderson-Hasselbalch for blood. [HCO3-] in mmol/L, PCO2 in mmHg (0.03 mmol/L per mmHg is the CO2 solubility coefficient). Multiply kPa by 7.5 to get mmHg.
PaO2 in kPa or mmHg and FiO2 as a fraction (for example 0.40). Record the inspired oxygen with every blood gas so PaO2 can be interpreted.

blocks.title: Worked example 2: taking and interpreting an arterial blood gas
blocks.prompt: Mr M, 68, with known COPD, is drowsy with a respiratory rate of 10/min on 28% oxygen via a mask. Describe how you would obtain a radial arterial sample and interpret: pH 7.29, PaCO2 8.4 kPa, HCO3 29 mmol/L, PaO2 10.4 kPa, FiO2 0.28.

steps.text: Consent (or best interests if he cannot consent), identify the patient and record the inspired oxygen. Palpate the radial pulse, assess collateral flow (a modified Allen test is commonly used although its predictive value is debated), choose the wrist without a fistula, clean the skin and consider local anaesthetic per local policy.

Use a pre-heparinised syringe, hold the wrist extended, insert at about 30 to 45 degrees against the pulse, allow the syringe to fill passively with pulsatile blood, withdraw, expel air bubbles, discard the needle into the sharps bin and apply firm pressure for at least five minutes (longer if anticoagulated or coagulopathic). Analyse promptly, label with FiO2 and temperature if required.

Interpret in order: pH 7.29 is acidaemic. PaCO2 8.4 kPa is raised, so respiratory acidosis. HCO3 29 mmol/L is raised, consistent with renal compensation for chronic CO2 retention. Check using Henderson-Hasselbalch: 8.4 kPa is 63 mmHg, so pH = 6.1 + log(29 / (0.03 x 63)) = 6.1 + log(15.3) = 7.29, which matches.

Oxygenation: PaO2/FiO2 = 10.4 / 0.28 = 37 kPa; the PaO2 is acceptable, and he is retaining CO2 on controlled oxygen. Management should follow local guidance for acute exacerbation of COPD, with senior review and a decision about non-invasive ventilation; oxygen targets and drug doses to be checked against BTS, NICE and BNF guidance.

blocks.answer: Acute-on-chronic (compensated in part) respiratory acidosis with adequate oxygenation: pH 7.29, PaCO2 8.4 kPa, HCO3 29 mmol/L, requiring senior review and consideration of non-invasive ventilation.

blocks.markdown: **Sharps injury.** Immediately encourage the wound to bleed gently and wash with soap and running water; do not scrub or suck the wound. For a splash to the eyes or mouth, rinse copiously with water or saline. Report at once to occupational health or the emergency department, according to local policy, because post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV works best if started as soon as possible, ideally within hours; the source patient's blood-borne virus risk is assessed and, with appropriate consent, tested; your hepatitis B immunity status determines whether a booster or immunoglobulin is needed. Complete an incident report. Prevention: never re-sheath, use safety devices, dispose of the item at the point of use in a sharps container and do not overfill it.

blocks.title: Documenting procedures
blocks.text: The record must let another clinician reconstruct what happened: date and time, procedure and indication, consent, operator and supervisor, ANTT, site and device (size, batch), number of attempts, complications, the patient's tolerance, results or volumes obtained, and the aftercare plan (for example catheter review date). Never document a procedure you did not do.

items: Record indication, consent, operator and supervisor.
Record site, device, number of attempts, complications and outcome.
For catheters, record the type, size, balloon volume, volume drained and the planned review or removal date.
For an arterial gas, record the FiO2 or room air, the site, the time and the pressure applied.
Report sharps injuries immediately and complete an incident form.

points: Every procedure starts with indication, consent, preparation and ANTT, and ends with disposal of sharps and a full record.
Cannula site and size depend on the clinical need; avoid arms with fistulas, infusions or axillary clearance, and review the cannula daily.

Catheterise only with a documented indication and review date, insert to the hilt and confirm urine flow before inflating the balloon, and avoid urethral catheterisation after suspected urethral injury.
A radial blood gas needs firm pressure afterwards and the inspired oxygen recorded; interpret with pH, PaCO2, HCO3 and PaO2 together.
After a sharps injury, encourage bleeding, wash, report immediately and attend for risk assessment and prophylaxis as advised.

questions.stem: Before venepuncture, which arm should generally be avoided?

options.text: The arm with an arteriovenous fistula for dialysis
The arm on the patient's non-dominant side
The arm with the most visible veins
The left arm in every case

questions.correctOptionText: The arm with an arteriovenous fistula for dialysis

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the fistula must be protected from puncture, infection and loss of patency.
distractorRationale.c: Visible veins are a good sign.
distractorRationale.d: There is no rule to avoid the left arm.

questions.explanation: A fistula or graft arm is avoided to protect dialysis access. Other arms to avoid include one with an infusion running or a recent axillary node clearance.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man becomes pale, sweaty and then faints during venepuncture. What is the best immediate action?

options.text: Stop, remove the needle, lay him flat with legs raised and monitor his pulse and breathing
Continue so the sample is not wasted
Sit him upright quickly to see if he recovers
Give a large volume of intravenous fluid

questions.correctOptionText: Stop, remove the needle, lay him flat with legs raised and monitor his pulse and breathing

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is vasovagal syncope; lying flat restores cerebral perfusion and the needle is removed to prevent injury.
distractorRationale.b: Continuing risks injury and ignores the patient.
distractorRationale.d: Fluid is not needed unless there is another cause.

questions.explanation: Vasovagal syncope is a common complication of needle procedures. The correct response is to stop, make the patient safe and lie them flat, and to check that recovery is complete before considering another cause.

questions.stem: Two days after cannulation a patient receiving an intravenous infusion complains of pain; the skin around the cannula is swollen and cool and the infusion has stopped flowing freely. What should you do?

options.text: Stop the infusion, remove the cannula, elevate the limb and re-site elsewhere, following local policy for the infused drug
Flush the cannula harder to restore flow
Cover with a dressing and continue the infusion
Apply a tourniquet above the site

questions.correctOptionText: Stop the infusion, remove the cannula, elevate the limb and re-site elsewhere, following local policy for the infused drug

distractorRationale.a: Correct: swelling, coolness and poor flow suggest infiltration; the drip is stopped and the cannula removed.
distractorRationale.b: Forcing a flush spreads the fluid into the tissue.
distractorRationale.c: Continuing infuses into tissue and may cause damage.

questions.explanation: Swelling, coolness and flow problems signal infiltration of fluid into the soft tissue. The cannula must be removed, the site assessed and a new site chosen; vesicant drugs require additional local extravasation steps.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man is in acute urinary retention and needs a urethral catheter. Describe the consent, preparation and key safety steps for insertion, and explain how complications are reduced.
markingGuide: Indication confirmed; explain the procedure, risks (discomfort, infection, bleeding) and alternatives; consent obtained and recorded; chaperone and privacy offered
Check for contraindications (blood at the meatus after trauma, suspected urethral injury) and allergies including latex and lidocaine
ANTT, hand hygiene, sterile gloves and equipment, antiseptic and local anaesthetic lubricating gel
Insert to the hilt before inflating the balloon and only inflate after urine drains, with the correct volume; replace the foreskin afterwards to avoid paraphimosis
Connect the closed drainage system, record the volume drained and observe for post-obstructive diuresis and haematuria
Document the procedure, catheter type, size and balloon volume, and a review date to limit infection
questions.explanation: A good answer covers consent, ANTT, the key technical safeguard of inflating the balloon only once the catheter is fully inserted and draining, and the monitoring and review needed afterwards. Marks are lost for inflating the balloon before urine is seen or for omitting a review date.

questions.stem: A man with a pelvic fracture after a road accident has urinary retention and blood at the urethral meatus. What is the safest approach?

options.text: Do not attempt urethral catheterisation; seek urgent senior and urology advice for imaging and, if needed, suprapubic drainage
Pass a urethral catheter gently using plenty of lubricating gel
Pass the largest catheter available to ensure drainage
Inflate the balloon early to hold the catheter in place

questions.correctOptionText: Do not attempt urethral catheterisation; seek urgent senior and urology advice for imaging and, if needed, suprapubic drainage

distractorRationale.a: Correct: blood at the meatus after pelvic trauma suggests urethral injury and blind catheterisation can worsen it.
distractorRationale.b: Gel does not remove the risk of creating a false passage.
distractorRationale.d: Premature inflation can rupture the urethra.

questions.explanation: Urethral catheterisation is contraindicated when urethral injury is suspected, because it can convert a partial tear into a complete one. Management should follow trauma and urology guidance.

questions.stem: An arterial blood gas shows [HCO3-] 15 mmol/L and PaCO2 30 mmHg. Use the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation (pK 6.1, CO2 solubility 0.03 mmol/L per mmHg) to calculate the pH to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: pH = 6.1 + log10(15 / (0.03 x 30)) = 6.1 + log10(16.7) = 6.1 + 1.22 = 7.32. The low bicarbonate with a low PaCO2 indicates a metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation, and the pH is slightly acidaemic because compensation is incomplete.

questions.stem: A patient on 60% oxygen (FiO2 0.60) has a PaO2 of 9.6 kPa on an arterial gas. Calculate the PaO2/FiO2 ratio in kPa.
questions.explanation: PaO2/FiO2 = 9.6 / 0.60 = 16.0 kPa. Because the ratio takes the inspired oxygen into account, it allows comparison of oxygenation across patients; a low ratio shows significant impairment, and thresholds used in classification (for example in respiratory distress syndrome) should be checked in current guidance.

questions.stem: After a radial arterial puncture in a patient taking an anticoagulant, what is the correct aftercare?

options.text: Apply firm direct pressure for at least five minutes, longer if anticoagulated, and then check the site and hand perfusion
Apply pressure for 30 seconds then release
Massage the site to disperse any blood
Apply a tourniquet above the elbow

questions.correctOptionText: Apply firm direct pressure for at least five minutes, longer if anticoagulated, and then check the site and hand perfusion

distractorRationale.a: Correct: pressure over the artery for at least five minutes limits haematoma; anticoagulation requires longer.
distractorRationale.d: A tourniquet can compromise the circulation.

questions.explanation: Arterial puncture bleeds under higher pressure than venepuncture, so pressure must be applied for longer. After releasing, check for ongoing bleeding and for hand perfusion.

questions.stem: After a needlestick injury you should encourage the wound to bleed and wash it with soap and running water, without scrubbing or sucking it.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Gentle bleeding and thorough washing reduce contamination, while scrubbing or sucking can damage tissue or expose the mouth. Immediate reporting to occupational health or the emergency department follows.

questions.stem: You are a student and sustain a needlestick injury from a needle just used to take blood from a patient whose blood-borne virus status is unknown. Describe your immediate actions, the risk assessment and follow-up, and how this and any procedure should be documented.
markingGuide: Immediate first aid: encourage bleeding, wash with soap and running water, do not scrub or suck; for mucous membrane exposure rinse with water or saline

Report at once to the supervising clinician and to occupational health or the emergency department, in line with local policy; time matters for post-exposure prophylaxis, which ideally starts as soon as possible
Risk assessment: type of injury (depth, visible blood, hollow-bore), source patient's risk factors, and the student's hepatitis B vaccination and immunity status

With consent, test the source patient for blood-borne viruses; baseline and follow-up testing for the injured person; hepatitis B booster or immunoglobulin, HIV prophylaxis, as advised by the specialist according to current guidance
Complete an incident report and arrange counselling and follow-up
Prevention and documentation: dispose of sharps at the point of use, never re-sheath, record procedure details including indication, consent, site, device, attempts, complications and aftercare
questions.explanation: The first aid steps and speed of reporting matter most because prophylaxis depends on time. The follow-up depends on a structured risk assessment of both source and recipient. Doses and regimens of prophylaxis must be taken from current specialist guidance.
